summary: A 1970 note with brief preliminary notes on the clock at the Augmentation Research Center at SRI. It is part of the early discussion of timing and measurement on the network.

eli5.summary: A short note describing the clock at one research lab, as part of working out how computers on the network should keep time.

subtitle: Technical description of the Augmentation Research Center's network clock system

tldr.problem: Network hosts needed accurate time references to support measurement and synchronization, but clock implementations were not yet standardized.
tldr.mechanism: The Augmentation Research Center built a clock system that stored both absolute time (date and clock values in core memory) and relative time (a running counter) updated at fixed intervals.
tldr.outcome: The design demonstrated practical clock implementation for network nodes and informed future timing infrastructure.

today: This is an early example of integrating precise timing into network hosts. Modern network timing is handled by protocols like NTP, which built on insights like these.

sections.title: Clock System Overview
sections.content:
The ARC (Augmentation Research Center) clock system at SRI provided a time reference stored in the core memory of an XDS 940 computer. The system offered two types of time information: absolute time (the actual date and time of day) and relative time (a running counter for interval measurement).

The absolute time was written as two adjacent core memory words, refreshed once each second. The relative time was a 24-bit binary accumulator that could be updated either every 100 microseconds or every 1 millisecond, depending on the application's needs.
sections.eli5: The clock stores two things: what time it is right now, and a counter that keeps track of how much time has passed.

sections.title: Absolute and Relative Time
sections.content:
The absolute time uses two core memory words with a binary format. The first word holds the month (1 to 12), day (1 to 31), and year (0 to 99) as three 8-bit binary fields. The second word holds the hour (0 to 23), minute (0 to 60), and second (0 to 60) as three more 8-bit binary fields.

The relative time uses one core memory word containing a 24-bit counter. This counter increments either every 100 microseconds or every 1 millisecond, allowing applications to measure short intervals without reading the full date and time.

The system provided long-term accuracy of about 1 second per 250 days through a crystal-controlled oscillator with standby power. Short-term accuracy was about 10 to 20 microseconds due to variable memory access delays.
sections.eli5: One part stores what time and date it is, another part counts ticks to measure how fast things happen.

sections.title: Practical Implementation
sections.content:
The design reflected the needs of early network hosts. The absolute time's accuracy on initial setting was about 1 second compared to radio time standard WWV. The oscillator had a drift rate of less than 1 second every 250 days. The system was backed by standby power to maintain accuracy across power disruptions.

The RFC notes that variable delays in accessing the 940 core memory meant that short-term absolute time reading was limited to 10 to 20 microseconds precision. This was acceptable for network measurement purposes, where the relative time counter could handle finer intervals while the absolute time provided synchronization anchors.
sections.eli5: The clock stays accurate for months, and even brief measurements are fast enough for network work.
